title: Resolving Power, Magnification and Optical Instruments
subcategory: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments — Microscope, Telescope, Resolving Power

references.label: NCERT Physics Part I, Class 12 — Ray Optics and Optical Instruments

summary: A compound microscope and astronomical telescope both use two converging lenses (objective + eyepiece) to magnify, but for very different purposes — a microscope enlarges tiny nearby objects, while a telescope brings distant objects visually closer — and resolving power (limited by diffraction) sets a fundamental limit on how much fine detail can ever be distinguished, regardless of magnification.
explanation: A compound microscope uses an OBJECTIVE lens (short focal length, placed very close to a small, nearby object) to form a real, inverted, magnified image, which is then further magnified by an EYEPIECE (acting as a simple magnifier) — total magnifying power is approximately the product of the objective's magnification and the eyepiece's, and is INCREASED by using an objective and eyepiece with SHORTER focal lengths. An astronomical telescope, by contrast, uses an objective lens with a LARGE focal length and large aperture (to gather more light AND achieve better resolving power) to form a real image of a distant object, again further magnified by an eyepiece — telescope magnifying power (in normal adjustment) is fo/fe (objective focal length divided by eyepiece focal length), so a LONG objective focal length paired with a SHORT eyepiece focal length gives high magnification, the OPPOSITE size relationship compared to a microscope's typical objective/eyepiece design. Resolving power is the ability of an optical instrument to distinguish two closely spaced objects/points as SEPARATE, rather than a single blur — it is fundamentally limited by DIFFRACTION (the bending of light at the aperture), not simply by how much an instrument magnifies; even a very high magnification cannot reveal detail beyond what diffraction allows to be resolved in the first place. A LARGER aperture gives BETTER resolving power (less diffraction spreading, per the Rayleigh criterion) — this is precisely why large telescopes use big objective mirrors/lenses: not just to gather more light from faint distant objects, but specifically to achieve sharper resolution of fine detail, a distinct benefit from simple magnification. This is a key, often-confused distinction: MAGNIFYING power (how much bigger an image appears) and RESOLVING power (how much fine detail can be distinguished) are different properties, and increasing one does not automatically increase the other — 'empty magnification' (enlarging an image well beyond what the resolving power can usefully support) reveals no additional real detail, just a bigger blur.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming higher magnification always reveals more detail — resolving power (governed by diffraction and aperture size) sets a hard limit on detail; magnifying beyond this limit ('empty magnification') just enlarges the existing blur without revealing anything new.

Mixing up which focal length combination gives high magnification in a microscope vs. a telescope — a microscope wants SHORT focal lengths for both objective and eyepiece, while a telescope wants a LONG objective focal length paired with a SHORT eyepiece focal length.

Believing telescope aperture size only affects how much light is gathered (brightness) — a larger aperture also directly improves RESOLVING POWER (ability to distinguish fine angular detail), an equally important reason large telescopes are built bigger.
examples: A compound microscope with a short-focal-length objective (a few mm) and eyepiece achieves very high magnification for viewing tiny specimens like cells.

A large astronomical telescope's big objective mirror not only gathers more light from faint stars but also resolves finer angular detail than a small telescope could, regardless of eyepiece magnification used.
genZNote: Resolving power: the real MVP — magnification without it is just an enlarged blur.
